# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

This paper argues for a specific architectural idea: shallow-angle helical slug streams running in a prestressed membrane guide shell can provide a prestressed substrate, an actuation primitive along the ring, and, by steering, a way to hold the shape of an active-support orbital ring.

The first key result is local. Helical curvature converts momentum redirection into distributed inflation pressure and hoop prestress, giving the membrane guide shell something closer to a real structural reaction surface than a bare straight lane or monolithic rotor picture provides.

The second key result is global. The same helical geometry enables a four-lane balanced cell whose lanes can be modulated to produce distributed tug fields while preserving first-order steady momentum balance. Those fields act along the ring. They suit vehicle and tether loads, tension management, and the trimming of weight that keeps the ring centered on the planet.

The third key result is about shape. A ring held up by momentum is an arch whose compression member is the streams' momentum flux, and if the streams follow the structure every shape mode grows. Steering each stream toward the mirror image of the structure's shape reverses the sign of that push and makes the ring a string in tension. With look-ahead, a soft stator hold on slug spacing, set points that adapt to steady loads, and stator feedback on the off-center mode, every shape mode of the reference ring decays except uniform breathing, which is stable and undamped, in linear models and in particle simulations that agree with them to a few percent. Loads that change are the harder test. Steering has almost no room for them at long wavelengths, and in the linear model the stators, through weight trim, have to hold the longest shape modes, at a cost in power, for the ring to carry a point load of even eight tonnes.

These results belong together. The prestressed shell without the balanced control cell is only a carrier. The balanced control cell without the prestressed shell lacks a good medium through which to act. Neither holds the ring's shape without steering, and steering has neither the reach to keep the ring centered nor the room to carry changing loads at the longest wavelengths without the stators. Together they form a coherent architecture.

A major motivation for the architecture is that straight high-speed lanes and simple monolithic rotors do not provide passive self-centering by momentum redirection alone. The stream pushes into existing curvature. The helical guide shell is therefore not merely a convenient geometry. It is a way to supply the reaction structure and actuation channels that a viable ring would need anyway, and the separately guided streams are what make steering possible at all.

The main actuation result can be stated compactly. A stationary spatial speed gradient changes lane momentum flux. In a mirrored counter-propagating pair, one lane accelerates while the other decelerates through the same fixed section, yet their structural reactions add rather than cancel. In a four-lane balanced cell, those pairwise tug fields can be placed wherever a force along the ring is wanted while maintaining first-order steady momentum balance. Placed in opposed sectors they shift the line along which the streams push, by millimetres and at a high price in circulating power, which is why shape is left to steering wherever steering has the room.

The next crux is no longer whether that primitive exists, or whether a ring made from it can be held in principle. It is whether the things the control scheme takes for granted can be built: a measurement of the ring's shape against an absolute reference, a guide whose force is commanded to within its two centimetres of room, and a distributed stator, power, and synchronization system that can command useful momentum-flux gradients while simultaneously maintaining lane phase, headway, lift, prestress, power balance, thermal rejection, fault isolation, and acceptable degraded modes. That is the natural next battlefield for the concept.

Macro lift still demands superorbital ring-tangential momentum flux, and the closure screens remain harsh. The sharpest of them now has a number. The helix's prestress is paid for in guide force, sixty times the supported weight at the reference prestress, and the loop of weight, guide force, drag and hardware closes only if the guides' drag is of the order of a hundred-thousandth of the force they carry. The present paper therefore does not claim a physically closed, thermally solved, fault-tolerant machine, and its dynamic proof extends only as far as its models. It claims something narrower and, I think, more durable: this architecture identifies a plausible internal prestress and actuation primitive that simple rotor-around-Earth sketches do not have. Even if the full orbital ring proves too hard, the paper identifies a new family of active-support structures in which moving momentum, tensile membranes, and distributed control are tightly integrated. The force balance, the shape instability and the steering law are not particular to the ring. They apply to arches and columns of momentum as well, and a ring round the Moon would meet them at a twentieth of the energy per metre (@sec-generalization).
